Background: KV cache, offloading and MP mode

embed.caption: background · GPU reuse, offloading, MP mode

paragraph.text: request starts with prefill: the model reads the whole prompt and builds up the state that every later token depends on. In full-attention layers that state is the keys and values of each token; in hybrid models, linear-attention and Mamba layers keep a fixed-size recurrent state instead. LMCache calls all of it the KV cache. Prefill is the expensive part
engines like vLLM and SGLang keep this cache in GPU memory and reuse it whenever a new request shares a prefix, skipping prefill for that prefix and cutting Time To First Token.
That reuse only works while the cache is still on the GPU, and contexts keep getting longer. Multi-turn chats, agents
and agentic RL rollouts with long tool traces,
and RAG prompts full of documents
all produce more KV than GPU memory can hold for long, so it is evicted before it can be reused.
keeps it alive by moving it to cheaper tiers, such as CPU DRAM, disk or remote storage, and loading it back on reuse, which costs far less than recomputing it.

Offloading alone leaves one weakness: when the cache lives inside the engine process, it shares the engine's fate, and a restart or crash can wipe it out. LMCache's multi-process (MP) mode removes that tie by running the cache as a standalone server on each node, decoupled from the engine. The engine focuses on inference and the cache survives worker restarts. The cache also
cannot crash the engine, its CPU work stays off the inference path, the engines on a node share one L1 cache in CPU DRAM, and an L2 tier such as local disk or S3 sits behind it.

Where in the fleet does a prefix live? And with non-prefix caching, which cached chunks does a request contain, at any offset, on any server, as when a RAG request reuses documents? Both questions need a fleet-wide index, not a per-node one.

While requests run, something has to decide where work goes and how its KV moves: which node still has room in L1, whether to load KV from a peer or recompute it, where to store new KV, and what to evict. Today each server makes these calls alone, seeing only itself.

Outside the request path, an operator or an RL scheduler wants to promote a prompt's KV into node C's memory before a traffic shift or the next rollout batch, demote cold KV to cheaper storage, move KV from a busy node to an idle one, pin a hot system prompt so it is never evicted, or delete one tenant's data. Today that means talking to every server one by one
Networking solved this kind of problem long ago by splitting the

. Routers move packets fast; a separate control plane learns the whole topology and tells them where to send things. KV cache offloading has so far been almost all data plane: moving bytes between GPU, CPU, disk and network as fast as possible. What is missing is the part that sees the whole fleet and decides.
: one standalone process that builds a fleet-wide view of every MP server's cache and uses it to enforce quotas, evict, pin, prefetch and look things up across machines.

embed.caption: the vision · one KV cache, one programmable control plane

paragraph.text: Our vision is one KV cache for the whole fleet. Every node's GPU memory, CPU memory and storage should behave like a single pool, so KV computed anywhere can be f

ed everywhere, whether the fleet is serving users or generating rollouts for RL. The MP servers stay the data plane that moves the bytes; the coordinator becomes the programmable control plane that decides what to keep, where to put it, and when to move it. Those decisions should be policies anyone can write and swap, so new workloads, new hardware and new ideas can change how the cache behaves

paragraph.text: The built-in eviction policy is a reasonable default, not the right answer for every deployment. One team wants an L1 budget as well as an L2 one. Another wants deletes sent to the exact server that holds a copy, because its L2 is local disk rather than a shared bucket. A third wants a placement policy nobody upstream has thought of yet. So we made the policy layer, the controllers, something you can add and replace without forking LMCache.

text.bold: Controllers may only depend on views.

paragraph.text: A controller asks for the views it needs (registry, key directory, usage) and gets the same shared instances everyone else reads. It cannot reach another controller. Shared
is what views are for; if two controllers need each other's

, they were really one controller. This keeps an out-of-tree controller from breaking when a peer ships somewhere else. For the same reason, views are not pluggable: which views exist is the coordinator's contract with every controller.

A control plane fails in two ways. It can go down, or it can stay up and quietly believe something false. The first is easy to survive here, because the coordinator is off the hot path: servers keep serving, and fleet features wait. The second is the dangerous one, so most of the design is about keeping the picture
through restarts, crashes and lost messages.
When a server restarts or dies
An MP server restart wipes its DRAM, so every L1 entry it reported is now a lie. The coordinator catches this with the
number. When the first batch from a new incarnation arrives, the gate
the old one: every consumer drops the L1 entries that server reported. L2 entries are deliberately kept, because those bytes sit on disk or in S3 and survive the restart. They leave only when a
A server that crashes and never comes back is caught by heartbeats instead. If it is silent for 30 seconds (checked every 10), the health loop removes it and fences its L1 entries the same way.
When events are duplicated or lost
Every server's stream is ordered by
, and that per-server order is the only ordering the design needs. Each server is the only writer of its own facts, so there is no global clock and no cross-server tie-breaking. A batch with an old
is a retry or a redelivery, and the gate drops it. Applying an event is also idempotent: storing twice is an upsert, and deleting something absent is a no-op.

means events were lost. The gate flags that server's slice as possibly stale and keeps going. With Kafka, loss is rare: the server's producer buffers up to 64 MB and retries in order for up to five minutes, so a broker restart delays events instead of dropping them.
The coordinator writes two files, because its state comes in two kinds:
Views and controller state derived from events: directory, usage, LRU order, gate cursors
Every 60 seconds and on clean shutdown
Immediately, whenever a quota or pin changes
Hit rate, until the fleet re-stores

Derived state is large and changes constantly, so it is written periodically; operator intent is small and irreplaceable, so it is saved on every change. The checkpoint also stores the Kafka offset that produced its views, and that offset is the only read cursor, so after a restart the restored state and the resume point always agree. Taking a checkpoint briefly pauses ingest, so the saved views are consistent with each other.

Every persistence failure is survivable. A missing or corrupt checkpoint means a cold start, not a crash, and a failed write is retried on the next tick. In the same spirit, if one view fails on a batch, only that view misses it.

paragraph.text: Like any service, the coordinator tracks request rates and latencies, for both the calls it serves and the calls it makes to MP servers. But those numbers alone miss its

Did any batches go missing, did a server admit to dropping events, and did any view fail to apply a batch? A failed apply means two views now disagree, and that is worth waking someone up for.
How long does a stored chunk take to show up in the directory, and has a server stopped sending events while still heartbeating?
When did the health, checkpoint and eviction loops last finish a pass?
Did it start, how much work is it doing, and what is it failing at?
A few rules keep this cheap and honest. Each component keeps one
snapshot, and both metrics and the status page read it, so they never disagree. Labels come only from fixed lists; per-server values are gauges keyed by

that disappear when the server leaves, and keys or hashes are never labels. And a scrape must never walk a whole index under a lock, because a slow scrape would stall ingest. Counts are kept up to date as events are applied instead.

never fails just because the coordinator is degraded, because Kubernetes would restart it and throw away its state. And there is no readiness check that waits for warm-up, because it would block the very events needed to warm up.

Each controller has an up/down gauge, so one that fails to start is visible at once, and a controller with its own loop reports when that loop last finished a pass. Each role then adds its own metrics. Eviction counts sweeps, keys selected, keys skipped and why (pinned, or no server can delete them), and delete requests sent or failed. Quota reports each tenant's bytes used against its limit, pins report how many keys are protected, and prefetch tracks requests submitted, in flight, time to complete and how many requested keys were actually found.

metrics. A replacement may add labels and metrics but never rename them, so swapping in your own eviction controller keeps every dashboard and alert working.

A full control plane needs six capabilities: state, lookup, policy, action, scale and reliability. The diagram
where the coordinator stands on each today and where it goes next, and the rest of this section walks through the biggest shifts
Views split across replicas and levels of a hierarchy
Prefix and non-prefix lookups over HTTP
Lookups cheap enough for the request path
Promote, demote, move, duplicate KV across nodes
Distributed or hierarchical coordinators across clusters and clouds
Warm standbys with no cold start

Inference workloads reuse KV in very different ways, and the biggest gains ahead come from policies built around them. Multi-turn chat and coding agents keep returning to long, growing contexts. Multi-agent workflows hand work between roles in patterns we can learn. RL rollouts sample the same prompt many times across many nodes, and RAG requests share documents at arbitrary offsets. Each pattern deserves its own placement, prefetch and eviction strategy, and each can arrive as a controller reading the shared views, with no new data path. The plugin model and record-and-replay make this practical: a new policy ships as an out-of-tree controller, and it can be compared, tuned or even learned against a real fleet's replayed traffic before it touches production.

Taken one step further, people need not write these policies by hand. A self-evolving agent could own the policy layer: watch the fleet through the shared views and metrics, propose a new controller, evaluate it against replayed traffic, and promote it only when it beats the current one, then repeat as workloads shift. The coordinator already has the pieces such a loop needs: controllers as the unit of change, replay as a safe test bench, and observability as the score.

Smarter policies need more ways to act than delete, pin and prefetch. Promoting KV into a node's memory, demoting it to cheaper storage, and moving or duplicating it across nodes would let a policy reshape where the cache lives, not only trim it.

As policies lean on the coordinator, lookups move closer to the request path and event volume grows with the fleet, so the cost of each call starts to matter. Today the coordinator speaks plain HTTP with JSON, which is easy to read and debug. Alternatives such as gRPC offer typed contracts, streaming for events and cheaper calls, and the MP servers already offer gRPC to engines, so the right protocol is worth revisiting as the fleet grows.

text.bold: Growing with the fleet, and beyond it.

paragraph.text: As fleets reach thousands of nodes and inference spans both serving and RL training, one process will not hold every view or make every decision. The coordinator itself may also become distributed, or even hierarchical: a coordinator per rack or cluster making fast local decisions, a parent above them setting fleet-wide policy, and warm standbys taking over without a cold start. The same structure stretches across datacenters and clouds, where cooperating coordinators place and move KV with bandwidth and price as inputs. The event-driven design makes this possible: every view is derived from ordered per-server event streams, so state can be split, rebuilt or moved by replaying streams instead of copying it.

Every step keeps the same shape as today: events in, shared views, pluggable policy, plain actions out. That shape is what lets the coordinator grow from a fleet-wide directory into the control plane for one KV cache across the whole fleet.
